judgments.label: false_positive
judgments.rationale: The element is the article's lead photo, a side-by-side montage of Flávio Bolsonaro (left) and Lula (right), and the main screenshot shows both men clearly. The alt names exactly those two people, adds the story's framing ('em disputa acirrada pela Presidência') and a photo credit, and repeats the visible caption. That is at most redundancy, not a 1.1.1 failure. The crop the model saw had a sticky ad banner ('... MULTI FAMILY OFFICE') over the top third of the photo, covering Flávio's face, and the in-image INFLEET ad over the bottom, so much of what it judged was third-party overlay. Even that crop still shows two men consistent with the alt.

judgments.label: true_positive
judgments.rationale: The element is a Taboola sponsored-content thumbnail (a span with role=img and aria-label 'Image for Taboola Advertising Unit') and is the only content of its own focusable link (a.item-thumbnail-href: no title, not aria-hidden, still in the tab order) to the La Galerie (Cyrela) landing page. The snapshot's accessibility name for that link is 'Image for Taboola Advertising Unit'. H30, a sufficient technique for 1.1.1, says that when an image is a link's only content, its alternative must describe the link's purpose. This generic label is placeholder text in the sense of F30: it says neither where the link goes nor what the picture shows (a rooftop terrace with lounge furniture over the São Paulo skyline). The text link next to it goes to the same URL and carries the ad title, but it is a separate tab stop, so it does not make this alternative serve the image link's purpose. Being third-party ad content does not change the result.

judgments.label: false_positive
judgments.rationale: The element is the icon-only WhatsApp channel link in the site header. Its SVG ('whatsapp-negative' in the site sprite) is the WhatsApp mark drawn as a brand-green #25d366 disc with the glyph knocked out, on the white header, and the measured 1.98:1 is correct. However, the 1.4.11 Understanding document treats brand logos shown in the brand's own colours as exempt under the essential exception. For a logo that is the only visible content of a control, it only advises that authors 'may choose' a higher-contrast variant or 'should consider' adding an element; it does not require one. WhatsApp's own green is inherently about 2:1 on white, so this is not an author-chosen low-contrast presentation. Requiring 3:1 here is stricter than WCAG as its Understanding document reads.

judgments.label: false_positive
judgments.rationale: The element is the WhatsApp share link in the article's floating share bar on the left edge. It uses the same 'whatsapp-negative' icon, a brand-green #25d366 disc with the WhatsApp glyph knocked out, on white (the screenshot confirms the colours), and the measured 1.98:1 is correct. The 1.4.11 Understanding document exempts brand logos presented in the brand's own colours under the essential exception, even when they are a control's only visible content; for that case it only recommends a higher-contrast variant or an extra element. The low contrast comes from WhatsApp's own green, not from an author's choice, so demanding 3:1 applies a stricter rule than WCAG's.

judgments.label: uncertain
judgments.rationale: The element is the icon-only WhatsApp link in the footer's social row. Its icon is the site's own outline redraw ('contoured-whatsapp' in the sprite, stroke hard-coded to #65D072), not the brand-green artwork. It measures 1.94:1 on white, and the screenshot confirms this. The 1.4.11 Understanding document exempts logos shown in their brand colours, but not low-contrast presentations that are the author's choice. It is unclear which applies here. This site-made outline in a near-brand green has essentially the contrast of WhatsApp's own green (1.98:1), which argues for the exemption. But its colour and style are the author's, which argues that it must meet 3:1. Competent auditors would split on this.

judgments.label: false_positive
judgments.rationale: The element is the 'SAIBA MAIS' call-to-action inside a Google in-image ad iframe labelled 'Publicidade'. It is a non-focusable div with role=link, nested inside the ad's real anchor, whose accessible name is 'INFLEET Monitore por Vídeo SAIBA MAIS' and which leads to the same ad click-through. The advertiser and the offer ('INFLEET', 'Monitore por Vídeo') sit in that same enclosing link. So the CTA's purpose, learning more about INFLEET's video-monitoring offer, can be determined from directly associated context, and the packet showed that ancestor. The nested pseudo-links are a role or structure issue at most (4.1.2), not a 2.4.4 failure.

judgments.label: false_positive
judgments.rationale: The element is Taboola's 'Leia Mais' control: an a href="#" in div.tbl-read-more-box inside the article, which carries the class tbl-forkorts-article. The article is clipped to a short preview: its box ends near y=1441, while its text runs on for about 3,300 px. This button sits at the cut-off, just below the lead photo and caption, as the screenshot shows, and activating it expands the same article. It does not navigate anywhere. On a single-article page, placed inside the article at the end of its visible part, 'Leia mais' says what it does: read the rest of this article. The checker saw it only in DOM order, after the tags, as a link with an unknown destination. What remains, a link used as a button, belongs to 4.1.2, not 2.4.4.

judgments.label: false_positive
judgments.rationale: The element is the first link ('Capa', title 'Capa') in the footer's Correio Braziliense column. That column is a list of the site's own sections, inside a header that also holds a 'Correio Braziliense' link to the same URL, and the link leads to the site's front page, as the destination title confirms. Two other 'Capa' links go to the print edition and to Revista Encontro. But on this site 'Capa' naturally means the site's own front page, which is exactly where this link goes, so its purpose can be determined from its text. Understanding 2.4.4 calls different text for different destinations a best practice, not a requirement. Any ambiguity lies in the other two 'Capa' links, not this one.

judgments.label: false_positive
judgments.rationale: The element is 'Direito e Justiça' in the footer list of the site's sections. It goes to correiobraziliense.com.br/direito-e-justica, whose title and heading are 'Direito e Justiça', the same destination as the side-menu link with the same text. The link text names its destination exactly, so its purpose can be determined from the text alone. The third link with this text, under 'Impresso', goes to the print supplement. Understanding 2.4.4 treats distinct text for distinct destinations as a best practice, so this link does not fail because another one reuses its name.

judgments.label: true_positive
judgments.rationale: The element is 'Capa' in the footer list under the 'Impresso' label. It goes to impresso.correioweb.com.br, the separate print-edition site (the live check shows a dated print front page), while two other 'Capa' links go to the site's home page and to Revista Encontro. Read on this site, 'Capa' suggests the site's own front page, so the text alone does not convey this destination. The only thing that tells it apart is the visual column label 'Impresso'. That label is a separate link placed before the list: it is not a heading (and H80 is only advisory anyway), and it is not in the same list item, sentence, paragraph or cell. The title attribute repeats 'Capa', and the other items in the list do not mention the print edition. No programmatically determined context gives the link's purpose, so the 2.4.4 claim holds.

judgments.label: uncertain
judgments.rationale: The element is 'Direito e Justiça' in the footer list under 'Impresso'. It goes to the print edition's Direito e Justiça supplement page on impresso.correioweb.com.br, which now meta-refreshes to a restricted-access page, while two other links with the same text go to the site's Direito e Justiça section. The 'Impresso' label is only a visual link placed before the list and is not programmatically associated, so nothing programmatic tells this link apart. Yet the text does name what the link leads to, the Direito & Justiça supplement, whose articles are also what the online section publishes. Auditors would split on whether 'print edition, behind restricted access' is part of the link's purpose that the text must convey, or a detail covered by the best-practice note on distinct text.

judgments.label: true_positive
judgments.rationale: The element is 'Úlimas notícias' (sic) in the footer column of the Lugar Certo real-estate portal. It goes to correiobraziliense.lugarcerto.com.br/noticias/noticias/, while an identically worded link in the Vrum column goes to vrum.com.br/noticias/. On a news site, 'Últimas notícias' reads as the site's own latest news, so the text alone misleads. The only distinguishing context is the visual column label 'Imóvel' (a link in a separate header element, not a heading) and the sibling items about property. WCAG 2.1 and 2.2 cite the same list item, not the same list, as link context, and the Understanding asks for context directly associated with the link. The title attribute only repeats the text. The link's purpose cannot be determined programmatically, so the finding holds.

judgments.label: true_positive
judgments.rationale: The element is 'Úlimas notícias' (sic) in the footer column of the Vrum vehicle portal. It goes to vrum.com.br/noticias/, while an identically worded link in the Imóvel column goes to the Lugar Certo real-estate news. On this news site, the text alone reads as the site's own latest news, which is not where it leads. What tells it apart is the visual 'Vrum' column label, a link in a separate header element and not a heading, and its sibling items about vehicles. Neither is in the same list item, sentence, paragraph or cell, which is the directly associated context that WCAG 2.2's definition and Understanding 2.4.4 describe. The title attribute repeats the text. Its purpose cannot be determined programmatically, so the 2.4.4 claim holds.
